core.text: To say *will*, Latin uses two different markers, depending on the conjugation: **the future (the 'will do' tense)**. The 1st and 2nd conjugations insert *-b-*: *amā-b-ō, amā-b-is, amā-b-it, amā-b-imus, amā-b-itis, amā-b-unt* (*lūcēbit* — it will shine; *habēbis* — you will have). The 3rd and 4th change the vowel instead: *-a-* for *I*, then *-ē-*: *dīc-a-m, dīc-ē-s, dīc-e-t, dīc-ē-mus, dīc-ē-tis, dīc-e-nt* (*faciam* — I will do; *dormiet* — he will sleep). *esse* has *erō, eris, erit, erimus, eritis, erunt*. Latin name: futūrum indicātīvī āctīvī.
English marks the future with *will* or *shall* (*I will go*) or with *going to*. Latin has no helping verb; the ending carries the *will*.

*-bi-* and *-ba-* are one letter apart: *amābit* — he will love; *amābat* — he was loving, the imperfect (the 'was doing' tense). And in the 3rd conjugation the future *-ē-* (*dīcēs, dīcet*) looks like the 2nd conjugation's present (*vidēs, videt*): check the dictionary form — *dīcere* (3rd) makes *dīcet* a future, *vidēre* (2nd) makes *videt* a present.

more.text: 3rd-conjugation *-iō* verbs and the 4th share *-iam, -iēs, -iet*: *faciam, faciēs, faciet; audiam, audiēs, audiet*. The future passive is *-bor, -beris, -bitur, -bimur, -biminī, -buntur* and *-ar, -ēris, -ētur, -ēmur, -ēminī, -entur* (*laudābitur*, *mittētur*). *īre* has *ībō*, *posse* *poterō*, *ferre* *feram*.

The *-am* first person of the 3rd and 4th is the same form as the present subjunctive (the 'may / let' form: veniat = let him come, may he come): *faciam* can be *I will do* or *what am I to do?* — the context and the next forms decide (*faciēs* is future, *faciās* subjunctive).

The learner's notes (week 20): like the imperfect, the future is made with an intermediate ending; for most verbs it is *a / e* — *a* in the first person singular and *e* elsewhere — with no variable vowel needed and *-m* for *I* (*pōnam, pōnēs, pōnet, pōnēmus, pōnētis, pōnent; fugiam, veniam*); for *a-* and *e-*stem verbs this does not work, so the marker *b* is used instead, after which the variable vowels stay and *-ō* is used (*pulsābō, pulsābis, pulsābit, pulsābimus, pulsābitis, pulsābunt; vidēbō*). Ørberg (chapter XX): futūrum *-bit / -bunt* and *-et / -ent*; *computābit, pārēbit, scrībet, dormiet*; *erō, eris, erit*; *crās rūrsus in lūdō dormiēs, male computābis, foedē scrībēs*.

teach.title: What the tense does
teach.say: For what has not happened yet Latin uses the future (the 'will do' tense): *crās Iūlius ambulābit*, tomorrow Julius will walk. It is one word, with no helper like the English 'will'. Words such as *crās* 'tomorrow' and *mox* 'soon' often stand beside it, but the tense itself is carried by the verb alone.

check.ask: Tap the verb that has not happened yet.

teach.title: 1st and 2nd conjugations: the endings -bit and -bunt
teach.say: Verbs of the first and second conjugations (the conjugation is which of the four families a Latin verb belongs to) build the future with a *-b-*: stem + bi + ending. For he, she or it that comes out as *-bit* (*ambulābit*, *vidēbit*); for they it is *-bunt* (*cantābunt*, *tacēbunt*). Only these two conjugations use the *-b-*, and it makes their future the easiest one to spot.

show.say: ambulābit, ambulābunt — the -b- of the first conjugation

check.ask: Now the same two cells on vocō: the future for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: The other persons, and -bō for 'I'
teach.say: The rest follow the same shape: *-bis* for you, *-bimus* for we, *-bitis* for you all. The 'I' form drops the vowel and ends in *-bō*: *ambulābō*, I will walk. Notice that the imperfect's 'I' ended in *-m* and the future's ends in *-ō* — the quickest way to keep the two apart.

check.ask: Write the future of laudō for I, for you, for we and for you all.

teach.title: 3rd and 4th conjugations: -am, then -ē- everywhere else
teach.say: Third- and fourth-conjugation verbs use no *-b-* at all. Their 'I' form ends in *-am*, and every other person has an *-ē-*: *scrībēs, scrībēmus, scrībētis*. Before a final *-t* or *-nt* that *ē* shortens, which is why 'he' is *scrībet* and 'they' is *scrībent*. Fourth-conjugation verbs do the same: *veniam*, *veniet*. One verb therefore has two different-looking futures, and both belong to the same column.

show.say: scrībam for 'I'; scrībet, scrībent for the rest

check.ask: Now the same three cells on mittō: the future for I, for 'he' and for 'they'.

teach.title: Telling pōnet from pōnit
teach.say: In the third conjugation one vowel is the whole tense: *pōnit* is 'he puts', *pōnet* is 'he will put'; *mittit* is 'he sends', *mittet* is 'he will send'. Read the vowel that comes just before the ending, and let a word like *crās* or *mox* confirm what you found.

check.ask: Tap the verb that is about tomorrow, not about now.

teach.title: Using it
teach.say: Two futures often run side by side in one sentence, one from each pattern: *Dāvus saccum portābit et in mēnsā pōnet* — *-bit* from the first conjugation, *-et* from the third. Build them yourself, and let the verb's conjugation decide which future you need before you write the ending.

check.ask: Fill the blank with the future of agō, third person singular.
